newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Schiphol users seek government action on flight ban.
newsitem.headline: Schiphol users seek government action on flight ban.

text.p: Key players in the Dutch airline and airfreight industry called on Wednesday for the government to stop proposals by Schiphol airport for a night-time ban from August 1 on wide-body aircraft including freighters.
The proposed ban covers aircraft such as the McDonnell Douglas DC-10 and the Boeing 747 in its 100, 200, 300 and SP versions between 2300 and 0600 local (2100 to 0400 gmt).
A Dutch Transport ministry spokesman later added that a decision by the government is expected in the near future and by August 7 at the latest.

Meanwhile a meeting of Schiphol's management committee is due to meet later today to discuss which measures to stay within noise levels can be taken without government approval and whether the airport is authorised to unilaterally implement a nighttime ban.

Representatives of airlines, including KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, its 50 percent subsidiary Martinair, Air Holland Charter BV, El Al and Transavia Airlines (also 80 percent owned by KLM) voiced their concern at today's meeting organised by the country's Transport ministry.

Martinair spokesman Gerard Draai, said if the Dutch airport's proposals are implemented, then hundreds of thousands of Dutch holidaymakers will be affected. He asked what was the airport to do in cases where there were delays?
"If an aircraft is delayed does it have to sit on the ground all night with 300 passengers and crew?"
A Dutch Travel Agents Association spokesman described the proposals as:" totally unacceptable " and passengers will face problems if the ban goes into effect on August 1, he said.

Air Holland chairman M.van der Berckel said: "The August 1 deadline is absolutely impossible for a charter airline....Airlines need at least six months notice and Air Holland would be able to make changes for the schedule starting April 1 next year," he added.

A Transavia executive said the charter airline had been: " raided by Schiphol employees" in early July asking if the airline could substantially reduce its activities during the period covered by the proposed ban by August 1.

He added that it was not that the airline is not concerned about environmental matters, but that it was simply impossible to carry out such a move due to contractual obligations to customers and tour operators.
"This is not a pleasant way to do business," he added and sought a transitional period during which all the arguments could be reviewed before any proposals were implemented.
Has de Gong, Dutch shippers' organisation chairman, said he was surprised Schiphol had not mentioned the impact of the proposals on business.
The airport is a major distribution hub for many companies and the moves would result in drastic cutbacks in jobs and business activity in the Netherlands, he added.

Schiphol airport director, Rued Uylenhoet, added there could be a further meeting for all interested parties where other measures to soften the pain caused by the proposed measures could be discussed.
This could include adapting aircraft take-off weights, he added.
